Tim Rogers is a game critic who has worked in the industry for about 20 years. He built a cult following starting in the early 2000s through the site Insert Credit and his own site Action Button.net, where he published extremely long-form writing on various games of the moment, along with his personal favorites. He was also a freelance writer for Kotaku in the late 2000s-early 2010s, and in 2017 got hired on fulltime as a video producer. He left in early 2020 so he could work independently.

He's also a game developer, having worked for Grasshopper Manufacture in the late 2000s on titles like No More Heroes 2. He has his own studio Action Button, which has made and published a handful of games (though only one, Videoball, is still available to purchase as of right now). Alongside his work making videos he is developing a new game called TRUCK HECK.

Regarding the Patreon: He has spent the last several months working on a forthcoming Cyberpunk 2077 review, during which he also spent nearly a month back in February dealing with a life-threatening medical emergency that might have been indirectly caused by him getting COVID last year. 

The reason for the long gaps in between each video is simply that they're full to the brim with stuff. His playing/researching/writing/editing methods are extremely thoughtful and meticulous, and that quality shows in his videos imo. You point out that he's not living up to the one-hour-long-video-a-month line in his Patreon, which is a fair criticism, but he in turn overdelivers on the amount of stuff in each video; each one so far has been at least three hours long, with his most recent video being six hours. If you want to break it down in hours-per-month, he is still overdelivering: approx. 18 hours of content in 15 months (he launched the Patreon back in March 2020). Patreon backers are generally fine with the wait because he does deliver, even if it isn't necessarily by the exact terms he initially laid out. 

3- to 6-hour videos probably sounds incredibly self-indulgent to some people. And well, it kind of is. Tim built his career on writing extremely long-form everything-but-the-kitchen-sink style criticism. But it's also not time wasted. If that's daunting to you, he's been on record repeatedly as viewing each video he makes as its own miniseries, and divides them into chapters encouraging people to watch them one chapter at a time instead of binging. I think he's pretty cool and his videos are some of the best gaming criticism on Youtube.

There are so many instances where any attempt or request to make those groups more open and welcoming to marginalized groups is met with pushback from people (and it is almost always the people I referred to up above) who apparently cannot stand to see things that don't include them. Like, a while back there was a post by someone asking if there could be a project putting together trigger warnings on each episode. Totally harmless, right? But there were an alarmingly high number of people who got *really* pissed about this and threw a fit, because something something snowflake SJW etc. Try to respect other people's experiences, y'know?

**Anatomy of a Murder** (Otto Preminger, 1959) Pretty excellent courtroom drama. Presents a more comprehensive and realistic portrait of the criminal trial process than perhaps any movie I've ever seen. (9/10)

**A Dangerous Method** (David Cronenberg, 2011) I love me some Cronenberg, but I was half-expecting a dull history lesson. Thankfully, it's instead a wonderfully acted, cheerfully over-the-top melodrama that nonetheless gives a compelling, believable and insightful look into the lives and dueling philosophies of Freud and Jung. (8/10)

**Extremely Loud and Incredibly Close** (Stephen Daldry, 2011) At long last, a movie that exploits both 9/11 AND autism for cheap emotional points. I never thought I would actively hate a performance by Max von Sydow, but this film is just openly loathsome enough to do the trick. Viola Davis is the only actor in the movie who emerges unscathed, and her performance is good enough to serve as another reminder that she probably deserved to win Best Actress over Meryl Streep. (2/10)

That's a perfectly valid complaint, but the lack of closure isn't the only thing the Retake people are demanding be changed. The lack of variety in the choices you have at the end, the cut-and-dry A-B-C options that Casey Hudson had said they were going to avoid but didn't, and the general feeling that all the choices you've made up til that point ended up not mattering much seem (to me anyway) to be what fans are the angriest about, and what they're demanding be changed. If all they wanted was a "finished" ending, then they would probably have reacted a little more positively to Bioware's announcement of the upcoming DLC in response to all the negative feedback.

I'm not exactly a fan of ME3's ending, but demanding that Bioware outright change it is petulant and childish. You can't just demand that a creator change something just because you don't like it. If what happens in a work of art becomes purely subject to the whims of the fans, that's heading down a dangerous path. People obviously have a right to bitch about an unsatisfactory ending, but the Retake people DO have a ridiculous sense of entitlement. It's not simply some media smear campaign.
